report.name: Database Resource Usage
report.description: Who consumes the machine: CPU, memory (PGA), disk I/O, logical reads and network, per session, per user and per machine, plus the heaviest SQL and a per-instance load overview. RAC-aware (all GV$). Session/user counters are cumulative since logon, not a live rate — read them together with the current-activity snapshot.
report.analysis_instructions:
IDIOMA: escreva TODO o relatório em português (pt-BR). Não traduza jargão técnico consagrado (session, logical reads, buffer gets, PGA, wait class, SQL*Net etc.).

The line above defines the report's OUTPUT LANGUAGE. EVERYTHING is written in that language: prose, table headers, fixed labels and section titles. English titles/labels in this specification are meant to be TRANSLATED, never copied. Numbering, order and meaning never change.

This report identifies WHERE the machine's resources go — CPU, memory (PGA), disk I/O, logical reads, network — by session, user and machine, plus the heaviest SQL. Every query is GV$ (RAC-aware): on a multi-instance database each table already carries inst_id, so always report which INSTANCE a consumer is on. Each query's description starts with a tag [1]-[8] naming its section.

CRITICAL caveat you must state and honour: the per-session and per-user counters (CPU, logical reads, physical read/write bytes, SQL*Net bytes) are CUMULATIVE SINCE THE SESSION LOGGED ON — they are a lifetime total, NOT a current rate. A session connected for days outranks one that was briefly very heavy. So never call a top-of-the-list session a "current problem" from the cumulative tables alone: confirm with the current-activity snapshot (active sessions by wait class + active detail: is it ACTIVE now, low last_call_et, in a real wait) and, where relevant, note that a true point-in-time rate needs sampling over an interval, which this snapshot does not do. PGA (Top Sessions by Memory) and the active snapshot ARE live; say which figures are live and which are cumulative.

FORMAT (Markdown): each section title as a level-2 heading ("## 1. …"), title text in the output language. Blank line between titles, paragraphs, lists and tables. Tables ALWAYS complete Markdown (header, |---|, one line per row).

1. Load Overview (Portuguese title: Panorama de Carga) — start with the per-instance overview: on RAC, which node carries the sessions/CPU/LOAD; then the live active picture (how many active sessions, in which resource classes right now). One paragraph a manager could read.

2. CPU — the top CPU consumers (sessions, and which users/machines from section 7). Name inst:sid, user, machine and the CPU seconds; flag any that are ACTIVE now. Remember the cumulative caveat.

3. Memory / PGA — the PGA consumers (live) and the instance PGA overview: is over allocation count > 0 (target too small, spilling to temp)? Name the biggest pga_alloc_mb sessions and what they run.

4. Disk I/O — the sessions with the most physical read/write MB, and the SQL behind them (match sql_id to Top SQL). Real disk traffic is the scarcest resource; lead with it when it is high.

5. Logical Reads — the biggest buffer-gets sessions: CPU/cache pressure, usually a plan doing far more work than needed. Tie to Top SQL by gets/exec.

6. Network — sessions shipping the most SQL*Net bytes; a large sent volume points at unfiltered/unpaginated result sets.

7. By User and by Machine — who owns the load: the heaviest database users and client machines/programs. This is where you attribute the consumption to an application.

8. Top SQL — the heaviest statements (elapsed/CPU/gets/reads). Cross-reference their sql_id with the session tables so a heavy session and its statement are named together. Cumulative since the cursor loaded.

9. Recommendations (Portuguese title: Recomendações) — concrete, tied to what the data shows: e.g. a single session dominating CPU with a known sql_id → tune that statement (name it); over allocation count > 0 → raise pga_aggregate_target; one machine dominating → check that app tier; a logical-reads outlier → review its plan; a network outlier → add pagination/array fetch. Recommend nothing the data does not support. This tool is READ-ONLY: never emit a command that changes anything; a kill or an ALTER is a suggestion for the DBA to review and run manually, clearly labeled as such.

10. Queries not collected (Portuguese title: Consultas não coletadas) — list each NOT COLLECTED query with its ORA error and likely cause. If none: one line saying all were collected.

Final rules: use exclusively this run's results; on RAC always name the instance; distinguish CUMULATIVE from LIVE figures every time; cite real inst:sid, users, machines and sql_id; recommend nothing without evidence; professional, direct, didactic tone.

sqls.name: Instance — Load Overview
sqls.description: [1] One row per RAC instance: user sessions, active user sessions, CPU count and OS run-queue LOAD. The first place to look on RAC — which NODE is hot. LOAD may be empty on some platforms.
sqls.sql:
SELECT i.inst_id,
       i.instance_name,
       i.host_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gv$session s
         WHERE s.inst_id = i.inst_id AND s.type = 'USER') user_sessions,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gv$session s
         WHERE s.inst_id = i.inst_id AND s.type = 'USER'
           AND s.status = 'ACTIVE') active_user_sessions,
       (SELECT o.value FROM gv$osstat o
         WHERE o.inst_id = i.inst_id AND o.stat_name = 'NUM_CPUS') num_cpus,
       (SELECT ROUND(o.value, 2) FROM gv$osstat o
         WHERE o.inst_id = i.inst_id AND o.stat_name = 'LOAD') os_load
  FROM gv$instance i
 ORDER BY i.inst_id;

sqls.name: Load — Active Sessions by Wait Class
sqls.description: [1] What the ACTIVE user sessions are doing RIGHT NOW, grouped per instance by resource class (ON CPU vs User I/O vs Network vs Concurrency...). This is the live picture; the resource tables below are cumulative history.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       CASE WHEN s.wait_class = 'Idle' OR s.wait_class IS NULL
            THEN 'ON CPU / not in a wait' ELSE s.wait_class END resource_class,
       COUNT(*) active_sessions
  FROM gv$session s
 WHERE s.status = 'ACTIVE' AND s.type = 'USER'
 GROUP BY s.inst_id,
       CASE WHEN s.wait_class = 'Idle' OR s.wait_class IS NULL
            THEN 'ON CPU / not in a wait' ELSE s.wait_class END
 ORDER BY s.inst_id, active_sessions DESC;

sqls.name: Load — Active Sessions Detail
sqls.description: [1] Every ACTIVE user session at collection time: what it runs (sql_id, event, wait_class), how long, and its current PGA. Names who is busy NOW.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       s.sql_id,
       s.event,
       s.wait_class,
       s.seconds_in_wait,
       s.last_call_et,
       ROUND(p.pga_alloc_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_alloc_mb
  FROM gv$session s
  LEFT JOIN gv$process p ON p.inst_id = s.inst_id AND p.addr = s.paddr
 WHERE s.status = 'ACTIVE' AND s.type = 'USER'
 ORDER BY p.pga_alloc_mem DESC NULLS LAST;

sqls.name: Session Resource Profile (top by CPU)
sqls.description: [2] The main table: one row per session with CPU seconds, logical reads, disk read/write MB and SQL*Net MB, top 30 by CPU. CUMULATIVE SINCE LOGON — a long-lived session outranks a briefly-heavy one; cross-check the active snapshot and last_call_et for who is heavy NOW. The app's table is sortable, so re-rank by any column.
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'CPU used by this session'
                      THEN st.value END) / 100, 1) cpu_seconds,
       MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'session logical reads'
               THEN st.value END) logical_reads,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical write bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_write_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_sent_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes received via SQL*Net from client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_recv_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('CPU used by this session', 'session logical reads',
                   'physical read bytes', 'physical write bytes',
                   'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client',
                   'bytes received via SQL*Net from client')
 GROUP BY st.inst_id, s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.machine, s.program
 ORDER BY cpu_seconds DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Memory (PGA)
sqls.description: [3] Sessions by CURRENT PGA (used / allocated / max), from gv$process. This one is live, not cumulative. Large pga_alloc_mb = sorts/hashes/PL-SQL collections in memory; pga_max_mb well above alloc = a past spike.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       s.status,
       ROUND(p.pga_used_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_used_mb,
       ROUND(p.pga_alloc_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_alloc_mb,
       ROUND(p.pga_max_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_max_mb,
       s.sql_id
  FROM gv$session s
  JOIN gv$process p ON p.inst_id = s.inst_id AND p.addr = s.paddr
 WHERE s.type = 'USER' AND p.pga_alloc_mem > 0
 ORDER BY p.pga_alloc_mem DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Instance — PGA Overview
sqls.description: [3] Per-instance PGA aggregate: target, allocated, in use, max, cache hit % and OVER-ALLOCATION count. over allocation count > 0 = PGA target too small for the workload (work spilled to temp).
sqls.sql:
SELECT p.inst_id,
       p.name,
       CASE WHEN p.unit = 'bytes' THEN ROUND(p.value / 1048576, 1)
            ELSE p.value END value,
       CASE WHEN p.unit = 'bytes' THEN 'MB' ELSE p.unit END unit
  FROM gv$pgastat p
 WHERE p.name IN ('aggregate PGA target parameter', 'total PGA allocated',
                  'total PGA inuse', 'maximum PGA allocated',
                  'over allocation count', 'cache hit percentage')
 ORDER BY p.inst_id, p.name;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Disk I/O
sqls.description: [4] Sessions by physical read + write MB (real disk traffic), cumulative since logon. The disk consumers; pair with Top SQL to find what they run.
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical write bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_write_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('physical read bytes', 'physical write bytes')
 GROUP BY st.inst_id, s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.machine, s.program
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes' THEN st.value END)
     + MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical write bytes' THEN st.value END) > 0
 ORDER BY phys_read_mb + phys_write_mb DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Logical Reads
sqls.description: [5] Sessions by session logical reads (buffer gets) — CPU and buffer-cache pressure even when data is cached (no disk). A huge logical-read session often means a bad plan doing nested-loop re-reads.
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       st.value logical_reads
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name = 'session logical reads'
   AND st.value > 0
 ORDER BY st.value DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Network (SQL*Net)
sqls.description: [6] Sessions by SQL*Net bytes sent to + received from the client, cumulative. High sent MB = a session shipping huge result sets (missing filter/pagination, array fetch off).
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_sent_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes received via SQL*Net from client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_recv_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('bytes sent via SQL*Net to client',
                   'bytes received via SQL*Net from client')
 GROUP BY st.inst_id, s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.machine, s.program
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client' THEN st.value END)
     + MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes received via SQL*Net from client' THEN st.value END) > 0
 ORDER BY net_sent_mb + net_recv_mb DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Resource Usage by User
sqls.description: [7] The same resources aggregated per database USER across all instances (sessions, CPU, logical reads, disk MB, network MB). Which application account owns the load. Cumulative.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.username,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.inst_id || ':' || s.sid) sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.inst_id) on_instances,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'CPU used by this session'
                      THEN st.value END) / 100) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'session logical reads'
               THEN st.value END) logical_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_sent_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('CPU used by this session', 'session logical reads',
                   'physical read bytes', 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client')
 GROUP BY s.username
 ORDER BY cpu_seconds DESC NULLS LAST;

sqls.name: Resource Usage by Machine / Program
sqls.description: [7] Resources aggregated per client machine + program — identifies the app server or tool driving the consumption. Cumulative.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.machine,
       s.program,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.inst_id || ':' || s.sid) sessions,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'CPU used by this session'
                      THEN st.value END) / 100) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'session logical reads'
               THEN st.value END) logical_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('CPU used by this session', 'session logical reads',
                   'physical read bytes')
 GROUP BY s.machine, s.program
 ORDER BY cpu_seconds DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top SQL by Resource
sqls.description: [8] The heaviest SQL in the shared pool now (gv$sql aggregated by sql_id): elapsed and CPU seconds, buffer gets, disk reads, gets/exec and the text. Cumulative since the cursor loaded, NOT since instance start. This is where a heavy session's cost usually traces to — match sql_id with the session tables.
sqls.sql:
SELECT sql_id,
       SUM(executions) executions,
       ROUND(SUM(elapsed_time) / 1000000, 1) elapsed_seconds,
       ROUND(SUM(cpu_time) / 1000000, 1) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(buffer_gets) buffer_gets,
       SUM(disk_reads) disk_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(buffer_gets) / GREATEST(SUM(executions), 1)) gets_per_exec,
       MAX(parsing_schema_name) parsing_schema,
       MAX(SUBSTR(sql_text, 1, 120)) sql_text
  FROM gv$sql
 GROUP BY sql_id
HAVING SUM(elapsed_time) > 0
 ORDER BY SUM(elapsed_time) DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;
